newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury deliberates on punitive damages.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury deliberates on punitive damages.

text.p: Jurors in O.J. Simpson's civil trial began deliberations on Friday on whether to force him to pay punitive damages for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend.
The panel met behind closed doors for just over two hours but failed to reach a decision, and Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki ordered members to return to court on Monday morning to continue their efforts.

In the culmination of three months of testimony in the wrongful-death case, the jury handed down a verdict on Tuesday that blamed the former football star, actor and TV pitchman for the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman and slapped him with $8.5 million in compensatory damages.
Before sending the six men and six women off for their second round of deliberations, the judge instructed them to reach their decision "without passion or prejudice."

Earlier in Friday's session, jurors heard an impassioned final summation from plaintiffs' attorney Daniel Petrocelli, who urged them to impose stiff punitive damages and declare to the world that "You cannot kill two people and get away with it."
But defence attorney Robert Baker contended that Simpson had already been punished enough and said anything more would effectively "destroy" his client.

Simpson -- who has steadfastly maintained his innocence -- was cleared of criminal charges in October 1995, but the victims' families pressed ahead with their civil suit, vowing that they would not let him get away with murder.

The compensatory damage that the jury awarded on Tuesday was payable entirely to Goldman's divorced parents for the loss of his love and support. But any punitive damages would also be shared with the estate of Nicole Brown Simpson, whose heirs are the two children she had with Simpson.
Petrocelli, accusing Simpson of cowardice for failing to show up in court Friday, implored jurors to "send him a message so loud that he can hear it on whatever golf course he's hiding out on."
But Baker contended that "Mr. Simpson has already been punished by the $8.5 million award" and said anything more would effectively "destroy" his client.
Petrocelli told jurors: "You are the last ones who will have the power to punish Mr Simpson for killing two people and walking away from it scot-free. I leave it to you to decide what is just."
"He can't come in here and face you, ladies and gentlemen, because you are the truth and you have declared that he is a killer," Petrocelli added.

As the trial neared its conclusion, Brown family attorney John Kelly made the day's only reference to a specific dollar amount for punitive damages, reminding jurors that Simpson had pledged in 1989 to pay Nicole Brown Simpson between $5 million and $6 million if he even hit her again.

Petrocelli, who represents the Goldman family, looked directly into the eyes of the jury and in a booming voice, declared: "You must send him a message that ... you cannot kill two people and get away with it no matter how much money you have, no matter how many lies you tell."

He told the jury that while they cannot send Simpson to prison, they had the power to exact a severe price. "He will get to enjoy the rest of his life as a free man while his victims lie in their graves," Petrocelli said.
Referring to testimony by a plaintiffs' expert that Simpson could make millions of dollars by cashing in on his notoriety, he said: "Make him pay, ladies and gentlemen."

Kelly asked the jurors to remember that any punitive damages awarded to the Brown estate would ultimately flow to her children, Sydney, 11, and Justin, 8, and that Simpson would not be able to touch the money.

Earlier in the session, jurors were told Simpson was unable to earn any money and was struggling to pay his bills. Leroy "Skip" Taft, Simpson's business manager, said Simpson's current earning capacity was nil and his future prospects were bleak.
Taft, a defence witness, gave the jurors a glimpse of what it costs to live in the world of the rich and famous, listing Simpson's considerable monthly expenses.
He said the mortgage on Simpson's mansion in the posh Brentwood section of Los Angeles was $24,000 a month "when he pays it," and the cost of maintaining the estate was about $30,000 a month.
